q: Identify the correctly spelt word according to British English standard.
e: 'Accommodation' is correctly spelt with double 'c' and double 'm' (two cots, two mattresses). All other options omit one 'c' or one 'm', which are the most frequent spelling errors in UP TGT exams.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the following options.
e: 'Separate' is spelt with 'a' in the middle ('a rat' inside 'sep-a-rate'). 'Seperate' is a common phonetic misspelling; derivatives like 'separation' and 'separately' retain the same '-par-' root.

q: Select the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Occurrence' takes double 'c', double 'r', and ends in '-ence' (from 'occur' + '-ence', doubling the final 'r' because the stress falls on the second syllable). Similar words: 'recurrence', 'concurrence'.

q: Which of the following words is spelt correctly?
e: 'Committee' contains three pairs of double letters: double 'm', double 't', and double 'e'. It is a high-frequency UP TGT spelling question alongside 'embarrass' and 'harass'.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Grammar' ends in '-ar', not '-er' (from Old French 'gramaire'). Similar '-ar' words often tested include 'beggar', 'burglar', 'calendar', and 'peculiar'.

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: Following the standard English rule "i before e, except after c" (when pronounced /iː/), 'receive' takes '-ei-' after 'c'. Other examples: 'deceive', 'perceive', 'conceit', 'ceiling'.

q: Select the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Embarrass' has double 'r' and double 's'. Contrast this with 'harass', which has a single 'r' and double 's'—both are classic UP TGT spelling traps.

q: Which of the following represents the standard BRITISH English spelling?
e: British English retains '-our' in words such as 'favourite', 'colour', 'honour', and 'neighbour', whereas American English drops the 'u' ('favorite', 'color', 'honor', 'neighbor').

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence showing possession for a plural noun ending in '-s'.
o: The boys' hostel was renovated last month.
The boy's hostel was renovated last month.
The boys hostel's was renovated last month.
The boy's' hostel was renovated last month.
e: For plural nouns ending in '-s' (boys), possession is indicated by placing the apostrophe after the final 's' ('boys' hostel'). 'Boy's hostel' indicates possession by a single boy.

q: Select the sentence in which 'its' / 'it's' is punctuated correctly.
o: The dog wagged it's tail happily.
Its a wonderful morning for a walk.
The committee submitted its report on time.
e: 'Its' (without an apostrophe) is the possessive determiner ('its report', 'its tail'), whereas 'it's' is the contraction for 'it is' or 'it has'. 'Its'' is never a valid English form.

q: Which of the following indirect questions is punctuated correctly?
o: He asked me where I lived?
He asked me where did I live?
He asked me where I lived.
He asked me, where I lived!
e: An indirect (reported) question functions as a declarative statement and therefore ends with a full stop (period), not a question mark, and uses subject–verb order ('where I lived').

q: Choose the sentence with correct capitalization.
o: We visited the ganges and the himalayas in winter.
We visited the Ganges and the Himalayas in Winter.
We visited the Ganges and the Himalayas in winter.
We visited The Ganges and The Himalayas in winter.
e: Proper geographical names ('Ganges', 'Himalayas') are capitalized, whereas names of seasons ('winter', 'summer', 'autumn') are common nouns and are NOT capitalized in standard English unless personified.

q: Identify the correctly punctuated sentence.
o: She bought apples, bananas, oranges, and grapes.
She bought, apples, bananas, oranges and grapes.
She bought apples bananas, oranges and grapes.
She bought apples, bananas; oranges, and grapes.
e: Commas separate three or more parallel items in a list without placing a comma directly between the verb ('bought') and its object ('apples'). A semicolon is unnecessary for simple single-word items.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Privilege' has NO 'd' and ends in '-lege' (from Latin 'privus' + 'lex/legis', private law). Similarly, 'allege' and 'sacrilege' end in '-lege'.

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: Although derived from the verb 'maintain', the noun 'maintenance' changes '-tain-' to '-ten-' and ends in '-ance'. Compare with 'sustenance' (from 'sustain') and 'abstinence' (from 'abstain').

q: Select the correctly spelt word according to British English.
e: 'Bureaucracy' is formed from the French word 'bureau' + Greek '-cracy' (rule). Remembering 'bureau' ensures the exact sequence 'b-u-r-e-a-u-c-r-a-c-y'.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Millennium' has double 'l' and double 'n' (from Latin 'mille' = thousand + 'annus' = year). Note also 'centennial' and 'biennial' which preserve double 'n' from 'annus'.

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: Borrowed directly from French, 'questionnaire' keeps double 'n' and ends in '-aire'. Similar French loans include 'millionaire' and 'billionaire' (double 'n' only in 'questionnaire').

q: Select the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Liaison' (communication or cooperation between groups) retains the second 'i' after 'a' ('li-ai-son'). Omitting the second 'i' ('liason') is the classic error tested in TGT exams.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Connoisseur' (an expert judge in matters of taste/art) has double 'n', double 's', and ends in '-eur' (from French). Compare with 'entrepreneur' and 'amateur'.

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Renaissance' (rebirth of art and learning) has a single 'n' followed by double 's' and ends in '-ance' (French 're-' + 'naissance').

q: Which of the following is the standard BRITISH English spelling of the word meaning 'a skilful movement or military exercise'?
e: Standard British English spells it 'manoeuvre' (retaining '-oeu-' and '-re'), whereas American English uses 'maneuver'. Similarly, British uses 'centre', 'theatre', 'metre', and 'litre'.

q: Identify the pair where BOTH words follow standard BRITISH English spelling.
e: British English uses 'jewellery' (double 'l', '-ery') and 'programme' for general/TV programmes (reserving 'program' strictly for computer software), whereas American English uses 'jewelry' and 'program'.

q: Choose the correctly spelt BRITISH English form for the noun meaning 'a formal written permission' and the verb 'to practise'.
e: In British English, nouns end in '-ce' ('licence', 'practice', 'advice') and corresponding verbs end in '-se' ('license', 'practise', 'advise'). American English often uses 'license' and 'practice' for both.

q: Which of the following sentences uses the SEMICOLON (;) correctly?
o: I wanted to go out; because it was sunny.
She loves classical music; her brother prefers jazz.
He bought three things; milk, bread, and eggs.
Although he worked hard; he failed the test.
e: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction ('She loves classical music; her brother prefers jazz'). A colon introduces a list (C), and subordinate clauses take commas, not semicolons (A, D).

q: Select the sentence that uses the COLON (:) correctly.
o: The four cardinal directions are: north, south, east, and west.
She packed: a coat, boots, and a scarf.
There are three virtues I admire most: honesty, courage, and kindness.
He said: that he would arrive late.
e: A colon should follow a complete independent clause ('There are three virtues I admire most:') before introducing a list or explanation. Never place a colon directly after a linking verb ('are:') or transitive verb ('packed:').

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence in Direct Speech.
e: When the quoted speech itself is a question, the question mark goes INSIDE the closing inverted commas, and no extra comma is placed after it ('"Where are you going?" asked Meera.').

q: Choose the sentence in which the HYPHEN (-) is used correctly in a compound modifier.
o: She is a well known author.
The author is well-known across India.
She is a well-known author across India.
She is a well known-author across India.
e: Compound adjectives preceding a noun are hyphenated ('a well-known author'), whereas when placed predicatively after a linking verb ('is well known'), they are generally left open without a hyphen.

q: Identify the correctly punctuated sentence containing a non-defining (non-restrictive) relative clause.
o: My elder brother who lives in London is a surgeon.
My elder brother, who lives in London is a surgeon.
My elder brother, who lives in London, is a surgeon.
My elder brother who lives in London, is a surgeon.
e: A non-defining relative clause providing extra, removable information ('who lives in London') must be enclosed by a pair of commas—both before and after the clause.

q: Which punctuation mark is used to indicate an abrupt break in thought or a dramatic afterthought in a sentence?
e: The em-dash (—) signals a sudden interruption, shift in thought, or emphatic parenthetical remark (e.g., "He promised to help—if only he kept his word!"). A hyphen joins compound words, while a semicolon links independent clauses.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Supersede' is the ONLY English word ending in '-sede' (from Latin 'supersedere', to sit above). Only three words end in '-ceed' ('exceed', 'proceed', 'succeed'); all others end in '-cede' ('precede', 'recede', 'concede').

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Vacuum' is spelt with a single 'c' and double 'u' (from Latin 'vacuus', empty). 'Vaccum' is a frequent trap in objective spelling tests.

q: Select the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Lieutenant' is spelt 'l-i-e-u-t-e-n-a-n-t' (from French 'lieu' = place + 'tenant' = holding; pronounced /lɛfˈtɛnənt/ in British English).

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence using the conjunctive adverb 'however'.
o: He studied very hard, however, he missed the cut-off.
He studied very hard, however; he missed the cut-off.
He studied very hard; however he missed the cut-off.
He studied very hard; however, he missed the cut-off.
e: When a conjunctive adverb ('however', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'nevertheless') connects two independent clauses, it must be preceded by a semicolon and followed by a comma ('; however,'). Using only commas creates a comma splice.

q: Choose the sentence with correct capitalization of titles and proper nouns.
o: The Prime Minister met president Macron in Paris.
The prime minister met President Macron in Paris.
The Prime Minister met President macron in paris.
The prime minister met president Macron in Paris.
e: Official titles are capitalized when placed directly before a personal name ('President Macron'), whereas generic references preceded by 'the' ('the prime minister') remain lowercase in standard British usage.

q: Identify the correctly spelt BRITISH English medical term.
e: Standard British English retains the classical Greek '-oe-' digraph in 'diarrhoea' (double 'r', 'h', 'oe', 'a'), whereas American English simplifies it to 'diarrhea'.

q: Select the correctly spelt BRITISH English word meaning 'profuse bleeding'.
e: British English spells it 'haemorrhage' ('hae-mor-rhage', retaining 'ae' and double 'r' + 'h'), while American English uses 'hemorrhage'. Compare British 'anaemia', 'paediatric', and 'oestrogen'.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Sacrilegious' comes from 'sacrilege' (NOT 'religious'), so the vowel order is '-i-e-' ('sac-ri-le-gious'), the exact reverse of 'religious' ('re-li-gious'). This is one of the toughest UP TGT spelling traps.

q: Identify the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Pharaoh' (ruler of ancient Egypt) is spelt 'p-h-a-r-a-o-h' (with '-ao-' before the final 'h'). Reversing '-ao-' to '-oa-' ('Pharoah') is the classic error.

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Pusillanimous' (cowardly, timid) has a single 's', double 'l', and ends in '-ous' (from Latin 'pusillus' = very small + 'animus' = spirit).

q: Select the word that is MISSPELT in British English.
e: 'Pronounciation' is misspelt; the correct spelling is 'pronunciation' (dropping the 'o' from 'pronounce'). 'Inoculate' (one 'n'), 'dissatisfied' (double 's'), and 'mischievous' (no 'i' after 'v') are all correctly spelt.

q: Identify the ONLY correctly spelt word among the four options.
e: 'Indispensable' (ending in '-able') is correctly spelt. Corrections: 'idiosyncrasy' ('-sy', not '-cy'), 'irresistible' ('-ible'), and 'inadvertent' ('-ent').

q: Choose the correctly spelt word.
e: 'Chauffeur' (a private motor-car driver, from French) has 'au', double 'f', and ends in '-eur'. Similar French '-eur' loans: 'amateur', 'entrepreneur', 'connoisseur', 'saboteur'.

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence containing a complex series with internal commas.
o: The delegates came from Agra, Uttar Pradesh, Jaipur, Rajasthan, and Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
The delegates came from Agra, Uttar Pradesh; Jaipur, Rajasthan; and Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
The delegates came from Agra; Uttar Pradesh, Jaipur; Rajasthan, and Bhopal; Madhya Pradesh.
The delegates came from Agra: Uttar Pradesh; Jaipur: Rajasthan; and Bhopal: Madhya Pradesh.
e: When list items themselves contain internal commas (City, State), semicolons must be used as 'super-commas' to separate the major items clearly without ambiguity.

q: Which sentence correctly indicates that Kavita and Neha jointly own ONE single house together?
o: Kavita's and Neha's house is near the lake.
Kavita and Neha's house is near the lake.
Kavita and Neha house's is near the lake.
Kavita's and Neha house is near the lake.
e: For joint possession of a single object, the apostrophe + 's' is attached ONLY to the final noun ('Kavita and Neha's house'). 'Kavita's and Neha's houses' indicates two separate houses owned individually.

q: Identify the sentence punctuated correctly with parentheses.
o: He finally answered after five minutes (he had been thinking carefully.).
He finally answered after five minutes (he had been thinking carefully).
He finally answered after five minutes. (He had been thinking carefully).
He finally answered after five minutes (He had been thinking carefully.)
e: When a parenthetical clause is embedded inside a larger sentence, the full stop goes OUTSIDE the closing parenthesis and the first word inside is lowercase (B). A full stop goes inside only when the entire sentence stands independently inside parentheses.

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence containing a quotation within a quotation (British/Standard convention).
o: He said, "My teacher always told us, "Honesty is the best policy.""
He said, "My teacher always told us, 'Honesty is the best policy.'"
He said, "My teacher always told us, 'Honesty is the best policy'."
He said, 'My teacher always told us, 'Honesty is the best policy.''
e: A quotation embedded inside another quotation uses alternating quotation marks—single quotes inside double quotes (or double inside single in strict British publishing)—with the terminal period neatly closing the inner statement without double-marking.

q: Which of the following sentences is FREE from a comma splice error?
o: The sun set, the sky turned crimson.
The sun set; the sky turned crimson.
The sun set, therefore the sky turned crimson.
The sun set, however the sky remained bright.
e: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma creates a 'comma splice' (A, C, D). Correcting it requires a semicolon (B), a full stop, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: ', and').

q: In which sentence is the hyphen ESSENTIAL to preserve the intended meaning 'to press/recover an old chair again'?
o: He decided to recover the antique sofa.
He decided to re-cover the antique sofa.
He decided to re cover the antique sofa.
He decided to recover-the antique sofa.
e: A hyphen distinguishes homographs formed with the prefix 're-': 're-cover' means 'to cover again', whereas 'recover' means 'to regain health or retrieve something lost'. Compare 're-sign' vs 'resign' and 're-create' vs 'recreate'.

q: Identify the correctly spelt literary term meaning 'the formation of a word from a sound associated with what is named'.
e: 'Onomatopoeia' (words imitating natural sounds, e.g., 'buzz', 'hiss', 'murmur') is spelt 'o-n-o-m-a-t-o-p-o-e-i-a' (from Greek 'onoma' = name + 'poiein' = to make). It is a recurring UP TGT English favourite combining literary terms with spelling.
